title: CSP and Browser Security Headers
description: Learn how Content Security Policy and other browser security headers create a powerful defense-in-depth layer. Configure CSP in .NET middleware, use nonces for inline scripts, and understand the role of HSTS and X-Frame-Options.

data.text: Browser security headers are HTTP response headers that tell the browser how to behave. They are the application's way of setting rules that the browser enforces automatically. Even if your application has a bug — like an unescaped input field — a strong header configuration can stop the attack before the browser executes the malicious code.

Content Security Policy is the most important security header available today. It lets you create an allowlist of sources from which the browser is allowed to load scripts, styles, images, fonts, and other resources. Anything not on the list is blocked. A well-configured CSP can prevent injected scripts from running even if an attacker found an XSS vulnerability.

terms.definition: An HTTP header that restricts the sources from which a page can load resources such as scripts, styles, and images.
A random value generated per request that the server includes in the CSP header and in a script tag, allowing only that specific script to execute.
HTTP Strict Transport Security: a header that forces the browser to use HTTPS for future requests to the same domain.

data.title: Strict CSP with nonces
data.content: This .NET middleware adds a CSP header that only allows scripts with a valid nonce, plus Google Analytics and Google Tag Manager.

data.title: CSP is not a substitute for output encoding
data.text: CSP is a powerful second line of defense, not a replacement for proper output encoding. If you stop encoding because you have CSP, a single mistake in your policy will leave you exposed. Always encode output first, then add CSP on top.

CSP handles resource loading, but other headers protect against different attack vectors. **X-Frame-Options** prevents clickjacking by stopping other sites from embedding your pages in invisible iframes. **X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff** stops browsers from guessing MIME types, which prevents certain script injection attacks. **Referrer-Policy** controls how much URL information is shared when users navigate away from your site.

data.title: Security headers in ASP.NET Core
data.content: Add common security headers using the ASP.NET Core Security Headers package or custom middleware.

data.text: If your page needs inline scripts — for example, to pass a server-side configuration object to JavaScript — use a nonce. The server generates a random value for each request, includes it in the CSP header, and adds it to the script tag. The browser blocks any script without a matching nonce, so an attacker's injected script cannot run.

data.title: Razor page with a CSP nonce
data.content: The nonce is generated in middleware and stored in HttpContext.Items, then read in the Razor layout.
data.code:
<!-- In _Layout.cshtml -->
<script nonce="@Context.Items["CspNonce"]">
  window.APP_CONFIG = @Html.Raw(JsonSerializer.Serialize(Model.Config));
</script>

<!-- In React, read the config -->
const config = window.APP_CONFIG;
console.log('API base:', config.apiBase);

items.text: Deploy a strict Content Security Policy in production.
items.hint: Start with report-only mode to identify what breaks, then switch to enforce mode.

items.text: Use nonces instead of unsafe-inline for scripts.
items.hint: unsafe-inline defeats most of CSP's protection against XSS.

items.text: Set X-Frame-Options to DENY unless you specifically need framing.
items.hint: Clickjacking can steal clicks and credentials without any visible warning.

items.text: Enable HSTS with a long max-age and includeSubDomains.
items.hint: HSTS prevents SSL stripping attacks after the first secure visit.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: CSP creates an allowlist of trusted resource sources and blocks everything else.
Nonces allow specific inline scripts while keeping the policy strict.
Security headers like HSTS, X-Frame-Options, and X-Content-Type-Options protect against different attack vectors.
Headers provide defense-in-depth but do not replace secure coding practices.
data.takeaway: Layer your defenses: code securely, add CSP, then lock down with security headers.
